subsubtopic: CARRIAGE OF HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-INSTALLATION OF HOTBOX DETECTORS ON LONDON TO TORONTO TRACK-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. I refer to the daily threat facing thousands of people resulting from the refusal by the Canadian Pacific Railway to instal simple, basic safety devices called hotbox detectors on its London to Toronto track. Every day CPR transports deadly and inflammable gases on this track. We have already experienced one massive derailment in Mississauga. These devices are not required by regulation nor are they foolproof, but if they had been in place last November, the train crew might have had a vital extra warning that a derailment was about to occur.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Garant):
That this House deplores this threat posed by CPR's lack of proper safety signalling devices; that CPR be directed to cease the transportation of deadly and inflammable gases on this route until it instals hotbox detectors, and that CPR be directed to start the installation of these hotbox detectors at once.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. I wonder if he would explain to the House the complete reversal by the government in not providing funds to the city of Winnipeg for CP rail relocation. The Prime Minister stated that he favoured rail relocation. The Minister of Employment and Immigration stated that we need rail relocation. The predecessor to the Minister of Transport, Mr. Lang, said that we must have rail relocation. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River gave advice to the city of Winnipeg on how to obtain funds for rail relocation. In view of these statements, can the minister explain to the House the complete reversal of policy of the Liberal government?

April 25, 1980
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: WINNIPEG-RAIL RELOCATION-SUGGESTED REVERSAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Transport is in favour of relocation, and everybody and his aunt is in favour of relocation. This is the essence of it. Everybody finds it easy to agree with this relocation project.
A study has been made which illustrates or demonstrates the substantial difference between building overpasses and relocating, and the difference is between $65 million and $135 million. Three orders of government have some responsibility in this matter, and the city of Winnipeg is trying to find if it can get the necessary money for the relocation option from somewhere. The mayor and his advisers came to see us yesterday. As Minister of Transport the only instrument I have is UTAP, the urban transportation assistance program. Under that program $9 million can be assigned for that, and arrangements have been made to assign that project should the city and the province-because the province has the main responsibility to decide-accept this recommendation.
We are looking for money elsewhere and there is a possibility that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion might make a contribution.
The difficulty, of course, is the size of the gap between option one and option two, that is, the difference between $65 million and $135 million. Even if DREE wanted to be helpful, they would require quite an amount of money to do so.
May I conclude by saying that this is a responsibility of all three orders of government. We are in a bit of a vicious circle because everybody is looking to somebody else to see what they are going to do. 1 tried to say yesterday what I thought as Minister of Transport.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, may I direct my question to the Minister of Transport? It arises out of press reports of a week or ten days ago emanating from the United Kingdom to the effect that the U.K. government was prepared to cancel the landing rights of our national carrier between western Canada and the U.K. Can the minister tell us where this matter stands, whether
negotiations are in progress at the present time, and whether or not Canada has taken a clear position and one to which it intends to adhere with respect to alternate rights being sought by the United Kingdom in this respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: REPORTED PROPOSED CANCELLING OF LANDING RIGHTS IN UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this question has to do with the entry into western Canada of foreign carriers, particularly the British. Negotiations have started on this subject and somewhat to our surprise-because we do not expect this from cool Britishers-the British negotiating team went to the press and announced that if the Canadian approach did not improve they would suspend flights of Air Canada from western Canada to Britain next year.
That is the situation. It shows how difficult these negotiations will be in the future. It shows, also, that the British, like everybody else, have a short memory and have forgotten that way back in 1966 some arrangements were reached that were advantageous to their side.

subsubtopic: REPORTED PROPOSED CANCELLING OF LANDING RIGHTS IN UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Would the minister take this opportunity to tell Canadians just what the difficulty is between Canada and the United Kingdom with respect to these freedoms? In particular, I would ask him whether or not this precipitate course taken by the United Kingdom was associated in any way with the difficulty we experience in maintaining a presence at Heathrow International Airport outside London, or whether it arises out of other negotiations and, if so, what are the factors that have contributed to this precipitate step on the part of the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: REPORTED PROPOSED CANCELLING OF LANDING RIGHTS IN UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I was told that Heathrow has not played a role in this matter. That is in the past. What is happening is simply the normal exchange between negotiating teams which have very clear interests at heart. I do not think we should be discouraged. These negotiations are very important in terms of Canadian and British interests and it is normal that the first steps should have been difficult. What is surprising is that they should have led to the British announcement.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to answer a question raised yesterday by the hon. member for Regina West, who alluded to a rumour that firefighters are no longer responsible for the evacuation and rescue of people in an aircraft which has crashed. This rumour stems from a review which is being made now of standards for firefighters. A draft which was issued became the subject of a leak.
The truth of the matter is that the role of firefighters will remain to save lives, property being secondary to that primary objective of saving lives. However, the question being refined now is how to go about it, and the regulation is trying to determine that. It says that firefighters will provide fire free escape areas by maintaining "fuselage integrity" and very, very complex things of this kind, but should crew members be incapacitated, then firefighters will enter the aircraft and help in the evacuation.
This is, it seems to me, a very worth-while attempt to define in regulation what is the role of firefighters in terms of priorities in their responsibilities.

MR. TOWERS-IMPLEMENTATION OF METRIC CONVERSION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege pursuant to the remarks made on April 23, 1980, as reported at pages 326, 327 and 330 of Hansard, by the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe) relating to the metric program, remarks which I believe to be misleading and not representative of the truth.
The minister would have this House believe that there was full and open debate on the implementation of the metric program and, as he said:
-there were ample opportunities for hon. members to discuss this when the legislation on metric conversion was passed in this House.
The fact is that there has not been a metric conversion bill per se debate in the House. The metric program was foisted on the Canadian people through the back door in a devious manner.
The metric program had its genesis in the white paper which was tabled in the House on January 16, 1970. As is the custom with statements on motions, our spokesman, Mr. G. W. Baldwin, had only a few minutes in which to comment on the proposal. A metric converion omnibus bill was not introduced or debated in the House. Bill S-5, the Weights and Measures Act, was introduced in the Senate in October of 1970 and was
Privilege-Mr. Towers
passed in April of 1971. The bill provided that metric units could be used in trade in Canada. It would appear then that the government established a metric commission by executive order.
The Minister of State for Small Businesses stated:
-the government has no intention of imposing the metric system-
But in fact this is what has been happening in Canada. Between June, 1971, when the metric commission was established, and November, 1976 when Bill C-23 was introduced in the House, there was no opportunity for hon. members to debate the principle. A metric program was already in place when Bill C-23 came before the House. Hon. members were presented with a fait accompli. Bill C-23 was simply a catchall bill facilitating amendments to several pieces of existing legislation, such as the Wheat Board Act, the Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act, etc.
On page 330 of Hansard the minister is reported to have referred also to progress in metrication in the United States. To the best of my knowledge, the government and business community in the United States has not taken steps to go metric. Perhaps the minister has information we do not possess and he will be kind enough to make it available to us. At the time of the tabling of the white paper, Mr. Baldwin said:
We should think particularly of our trading relations with the United States, which of course is and has been for some years examining its position with regard to adoption of metric. Whether we like it or not, what we must do to a considerable extent is to keep pace with what is being done in the United States.
I think it might well be suicidal for us to adopt the metric system without considering what is being done in the United States.
The minister has not given the House an accurate chronology of events which led up to the introduction of metrication in Canada. I believe that my rights, along with the rights of millions of Canadians who are in opposition to metric, have been infringed upon by the misrepresentation of successive Liberal ministers, including the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Lapointe).
After studying the case, Madam Speaker, if you rule that my rights as a member of this House, along with those of many Canadians resident in a supposedly free country, have not been upheld by the actions of successive Liberal governments, I am prepared to move, seconded by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil):
That the matter of the misrepresentation of the Minister of State for Small Businesses of the proceedings of this House on metrication be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

subtopic: MR. TOWERS-IMPLEMENTATION OF METRIC CONVERSION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to speak very briefly on this point. I noted that the minister indicated that it is indeed possible for a human error to be made by a minister or by others and he suggests that that was the cause of the information he gave to the House to which a complaint has been made by my colleague, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers).
It is my very clear recollection-and 1 have not had a chance to consult Hansard on that matter-that in fact there were two questions put to the minister, that there was a separation of time, and that he had the opportunity to become briefed on the matter. Indeed, he was provided with supplementary information having to do with the authority on which metric is based. The information of which the hon. member has complained was in fact a deliberate statement in his second answer, when the minister attempted to cite a number of pieces of legislation which he claimed gave authority for the implementation of the metric system. In other words, it was not a simple error based upon misinformation; it was a deliberate statement reflecting a consultation of the laws that had been passed and of the situation at the time.
I think the minister has raised the point that were there to be a simple error, the Chair might decide one way, that the Chair might decide that it was a simple error; but if a statement had been made after the minister has had the opportunity to consider the facts and if, in the course of that statement, he cited various pieces of legislation, as it is my recollection he did, then I believe the question of the hon. member for Red Deer for a reference of this matter is much more firmly founded.
As Madam Speaker will know, of course, there is a great concern in this House and indeed in this country that we are proceeding with reckless speed with the implementation of a program which has no, or the most suspect of, legislative authority. That is a side issue, but it is an important one. It speaks to the seriousness with which the question was raised by the hon. member for Red Deer and by others on this side of the House, and to the seriousness with which the country would react to a position taken by the government, deliberately or by accident, that in fact there was legal foundation for a system which we believe is being imposed without adequate
legal foundation. The capacity to consider the answer by the minister is very germane to Your Honour's finding.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)

Madam Speaker, I listened very closely to the remarks made by the right hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark). In my first answer, or that given to the first question, 1 recognize I was in error, because I had not enough time to be adequately informed. I quote from page 326 of Hansard:
First I should like to remind the hon. member that there were ample opportunities for hon. member to discuss this when the legislation on metric conversion was passed in this House-
1 recognize quite humbly that there has been no legislation on metric conversion that was passed as such.
In my second answer, when I had the opportunity to check further the available information, I indicated in this House that when the Weights and Measures Act and also the Labelling and Packaging Act were discussed in 1971, reference was made to the metric system, and I did not suggest that that was an act concerning metric conversion, but that within the framework of the discussions held on these two bills, hon. members had an opportunity to address the matter of the metric system. And if the right hon. Leader of the Official Opposition will read my answer again, as reported on page 327 of Hansard, he will see that this is what I said in the House.

Madam Speaker, at the outset I should like to say that I support what the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) has said. I suggest that if the minister examines page 368 of Hansard dated April 24, he will see that the hon. member for Red Deer gave notice of the question of privilege which he planned on raising today.
I listened to the questions put to the minister on Wednesday which are recorded at pages 326 and 327 of Hansard. Quite frankly I was very disturbed because the response of the minister was such that it would lead people to believe that at some time or other, and perhaps on several occasions, members of the House of Commons have had the opportunity of discussing the implementation of the metric system. This is not so. He referred to the white paper which the minister said received the support of all parties.
Also I suggest that the minister should examine Hansard of January 16, 1970. There were three speakers, one from each of the parties. While there was general acceptance, there was no over-all debate and no indication at that time that the metric system would be imposed upon Canadians without a general debate.
April 25, 1980

1 feel the answers of the minister were such that he has given the impression to the public of Canada that there was a general debate on metric conversion. As 1 said, this is not so. The debates were restricted. I believe my privileges as a member have been breached, and certainly I am in support of the question of privilege of the hon. member for Red Deer. This was the reason 1 was prepared to support the motion and to act as seconder.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. TOWERS-IMPLEMENTATION OF METRIC CONVERSION PROGRAM
speechtext: The hon. member for Capilano.

subtopic: MR. TOWERS-IMPLEMENTATION OF METRIC CONVERSION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 too should like to speak in support of the motion of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers). What the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe) has done in his statement is perpetuate the myth that the House of Commons, since 1970 or the tabling of the white paper, has given the Government of Canada, no matter which party, a mandate to implement or impose the metric system on the people of Canada. I sympathize with him in his new position, with the duties, paper work and study he has to do. In fact they are imposing it through governor in council or through members of a commission making deals with public servants in departments which have the power to implement aspects of weights and measures legislation or health of animals legislation that were never intended to impose a change in the measurement system on Canadians.
In 1975 the then prime minister wrote to the premiers of the provinces of Canada advising them that he had a mandate from the House of Commons to ask for their assistance in imposing the metric system across the land. If Madam Speaker examines that mandate, it goes back to some legislation in the 1870s when there was an act which allowed the Government of Canada governor in council approval for certain actions pertaining to the metric system. If one takes unbiased, independent surveys on this subject matter across the land by age group, one will find that the Canadians resisting this imposition exceed 75 per cent of the population.
If the House of Commons is ever to represent the people against governor in council imposition of deals behind the scenes, using acts that were not intended for that purpose, then 1 suggest that this motion has to be heard by Madam Speaker and placed before the said committee. The issue is very serious indeed.

subtopic: MR. TOWERS-IMPLEMENTATION OF METRIC CONVERSION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear hear!

subtopic: MR. TOWERS-IMPLEMENTATION OF METRIC CONVERSION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Surely Madam Speaker will allow this chamber to represent the people at large when the power being used is vested strictly within the bureaucrats of the Government of Canada, with the use of the governor in council and
Privilege-Mr. Towers
acts that were never intended for this purpose. If Madam Speaker does not accept the motion, then it behooves the government to submit to the House of Commons a metric conversion act where the advantages and the reasons for it can be explored and explained to the people of Canada.
I urge the House to support this motion.

subtopic: MR. TOWERS-IMPLEMENTATION OF METRIC CONVERSION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. TOWERS-IMPLEMENTATION OF METRIC CONVERSION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to make a brief intervention in support of the motion and the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) and so well articulated by my colleagues on this side of the House. I think it is important to get the whole question in context. I sympathize with the minister. The fact is that he has had only a matter of three or four months to be seized of this particular subject matter.
I think it is important for us to understand two basic principles. The minister should be fully aware of the background circumstances because it is important if we are to understand the responsibilities of members of the House of Commons. One of the basic principles is that the only reference to the House of Commons by way of debate was on a resolution brought forward by the government in which there were brief replies by representatives of each of the parties. As I say, this was only referenced by way of government initiative.
On reviewing the record, it would be interesting for the minister to observe that the spokesman on behalf of our party at that time warned the government respecting the question of the implementation and accountability of the conversion program. Mr. Baldwin pointed out with the forensic ability he has shown in his distinguished parliamentary career that the most dangerous aspect would be metric conversion taking place without ample consultation with the people involved, that is, the people of Canada.
The second point which should be brought to the attention of Madam Speaker and the minister is that one of the shortcomings of this particular conversion program has been the lack of accountability to Parliament, either directly through legislation or by reference to a committee of this Parliament. What it amounts to is this. The metric conversion commission is proceeding on the basis of a resolution of a most general nature, enacted in 1970 and passed by this House, which simply supported the concept of eventual metric conversion in line with developments around the world, which everyone understands.
We in Canada have a unique situation, as the minister well knows, with well over 70 per cent of our trade taking place with the United States. It is foolhardy for us, in terms of economics and in terms of public acceptance, to proceed at a pace that exceeds by much the conversion that is taking place in the United States.
This issue demonstrates the fact that if we in Parliament, as has been indicated by my colleague, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), are in fact to fulfil our respon-

April 25, 1980
Privilege-Mr. Towers
sibilities, we must have accountability in respect of government-initiated actions which have taken place under orders in council passed by the government.
I say to the hon. minister, coming as 1 do from western Canada, that the Speech from the Throne made some reference to the responsibility of members of Parliament to stand up and state clearly in this House those issues that are of some concern to western Canada. If the minister wants to deal with a western Canadian issue that does cause some concern across that part of our great country, he should pay very strict attention to this question of metric conversion. He should take the lead in terms of having the metric commission made accountable to Parliament, and he should in fact give very serious consideration to the introduction of legislation which will outline the timetable and procedure under which metric conversion takes place in our country.
I do not want to go any further at this time except to say that 1 think this is a valid subject and a valid motion for the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, where members of Parliament could in fact, from a parliamentary point of view, bring forward their concerns in respect of this particular initiative on the part of this government and the responsibilities of the minister in that regard.

subtopic: MR. TOWERS-IMPLEMENTATION OF METRIC CONVERSION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: MR. TOWERS-IMPLEMENTATION OF METRIC CONVERSION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to set a few facts straight. It is true that notice of a question of privilege was given on April 24, as evidenced at page 368 of Hansard, but if you read what was said carefully, the content of that question of privilege is not specified.
With respect to the comments made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil), there seems to be an apparent contradiction when he says that when Parliament discussed the issue in 1970, there was, and 1 quote him in English:

"A general acceptance of the principle".
[ Translation]
So it was obvious, Madam Speaker, that the House had to vote at a certain time in its history on the principle of metric conversion. And my colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn), indicated that, and I quote:

"An act was adopted in 1970 recognizing the broad principle of metrication."
[ Translation]
So 1 think my predecessor held my portfolio longer than I did and I wonder how it is that now they should think it has become a problem of national urgency that action was not taken at that time. An action taken by my predecessor was to delay the introduction of metric scales in retail stores and I intend, Madam Speaker, to make the same recommendation he made to my colleagues in cabinet.
As to the rest of the debate, Madam Speaker, we cannot rewrite history. There was a discussion on that subject in 1970. It is not your fault nor mine nor that of members of this House if none of them spoke about that and I think the whole thing is basically a matter of a difference of opinion.

subtopic: MR. TOWERS-IMPLEMENTATION OF METRIC CONVERSION PROGRAM
speechtext:
On the question of privilege, Madam Speaker; I thank you for recognizing me again. The Minister of State for Small Businesses alleges that the action 1 took on this important subject matter was limited to the postponement of the implementation of metric action as it related to weights in the retail sector for one year. That is not so, Madam Speaker. I think I have the right to point to the record.
We imposed in a very careful manner a metric overview board that worked very industriously for a matter of months on this whole matter. It made six individual reports and a final report. The report was submitted to me in the last hours of my privilege of being a minister. I understand that under the new Minister of State for Small Businesses the report is not going to be circulated and made available officially, which I think is an absolute shame because the people of Canada have paid quite a few thousands of dollars for a report which does represent a very fair analysis of the concern that exists at large in this country.
I would think that the minister's predecessor acted in a very responsible manner in not doing unnecessary damage to the work that had been put in place by the metric commission, but rather represented the people of this country and represented one of the matters that was causing extreme alienation in more than one region in Canada. 1 should like him to please understand that I think I acted in a most responsible manner in this whole matter and did not do anything negative to damage any area that had progressed beyond the point of retreat.
Thank you for allowing me to say that, Madam Speaker.

subtopic: MR. TOWERS-IMPLEMENTATION OF METRIC CONVERSION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. TOWERS-IMPLEMENTATION OF METRIC CONVERSION PROGRAM
speechtext:
I think at this point I must remind the House that we are in fact going well into debate, even to the point that members are expressing opinions as to the efficacy of those who now have responsibility or held responsibility before. I do want to remind the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), while thanking him for his remarks, that it seems to me he is essentially dissatisfied with the answer he got to a question he addressed to a minister during the question period. He knows that he cannot debate that matter under the guise of a question of privilege.
The subject is important. Everybody has recognized the importance and the seriousness of the subject and I am sure the House will at some time want to debate it. I am entirely in the hands of the House as to the time at which it would want to do so.
In support of my ruling that it is not a question of privilege I should like to refer to what Mr. Lamoureux, one of my predecessors, said in similar circumstances, circumstances that
April 25, 1980

do arise very frequently in the House. He said that a member who essentially is not satisfied with an answer that he received to a question obviously does not have a question of privilege. He went on to say:
The hon. member, with his long experience in the House-
I think that would also apply to the hon. member for Red Deer.
-knows that he cannot rise on an alleged question of privilege to make reference to an answer which has been given in the House. The hon. member may be dissatisfied with the answer that has been given and he may feel there is a contradiction. He is entitled to his opinion about such matters, but this cannot be raised by way of a question of privilege.
Therefore I must rule, having heard this discussion at length, that there is no question of privilege.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-17, to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, be now read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: It is my pleasure today to present before this House for second reading Bill C-17, an act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act. In essence, Madam Speaker, this bill will extend the Small Businesses Loans Act for two years and, by so doing, will become part of the reaffirmation of this government's commitment to support small businesses in Canada.
As you probably know, Madam Speaker, the Small Businesses Loans Act originally came into force on January 19, 1961 to make it easier for small businesses in Canada to obtain term financing. A major feature of this program is that loans are made directly between the borrower and the lender without any prior approval of the government. The government simply guarantees a loan transaction which takes place in the private sector and in this way supports and builds on the strength of the financial community. Since 1961 the act has been subject to legislative review on a regular basis and amendments have been made over this period of time to widen the scope of operations under the act.
At present, Mr. Speaker, loans may be made for (I) the purchase of fixed or movable equipment, (2) the improvement or modernization of premises, (3) the purchase or construction of new premises, and (4) the purchase of land.
These loans are granted in accordance with standard lending procedures and are fully secured. The maximum period over which they can be repaid is ten years.

Since 1961 almost 65,000 loans have been made, to a total value of over $1 billion. These totals are a clear indication that the Small Businesses Loans Act is an important source of
financing for small businesses. The program has been growing very rapidly in recent years. In 1979 alone, over $250 million in loans was guaranteed by the government, fully one quarter of the total $1 billion lent over the entire history of the program.
The program has a broad national impact and it has steadily gained acceptance by the financial community. A breakdown by province of the total value of loans made in 1978 shows that 24 per cent were made in British Columbia, 18 per cent were made in the other western provinces, 12 per cent were made in Ontario, 39 per cent were made in Quebec and 7 per cent were made in the maritime provinces.
As for lender participation, the program was originally established to operate almost exclusively through the chartered banks and to encourage the banks to do more lending to small businesses in Canada. Since the inception of the program, however, participation by lenders has expanded. At this time, participant lenders include not only the chartered banks but also trust companies, mortgage and savings companies, credit unions and the Alberta treasury branches.
The bill before us, Mr. Speaker, proposes various changes and does two things. First of all, it amends the present act which has been in force since July 1, 1977 and is due to expire on June 30, 1980, and furthermore it amends and extends the act for an additional two-year period, from July 1, 1980 to June 30, 1982.
First, the bill amends the act so that the authorized lending ceiling which was established for the period from July 1, 1977 to June 30, 1980, is increased from $600 million to $675 million.
Mr. Speaker, when this act was last before this House it was extended for a three-year period. It was thought that a lending ceiling of $600 million would be sufficient to cover the three-year period. This amount has proved to be insufficient. With the growth of the program which I have already described, lending is rapidly approaching the $600 million ceiling. Bill C-17 proposes therefore that the ceiling for the present act be increased from $600 million to $675 million so that all of the borrowing which is required by small business will be accommodated under the terms of the present act which expires on June 30, 1980.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-17 extends the Small Businesses Loans Act for a two-year period, from July 1, 1980, to June 30, 1982.
It has been usual in the past to extend the act for a three-year period. This year, however, the government is undertaking an intensive review of all of its financing support programs for small business. This review will be complete in the coming months at which time the government will be coming forward with comprehensive proposals for small busi-
April 25, 1980

ness financing. Therefore a more normal three-year extension seems to me inappropriate at this time, Mr. Speaker, whereas a shorter two-year extension will more closely coincide with the conclusion of the government's review of its small business financing.
That is the main reason for the two-year extension, Mr. Speaker. I will return to make mention of the review by the government of the financing and of its support programs for small business at the conclusion of my remarks.
Now, I want to spell out the main amendments which are to be made to the act.

Most importantly, the limit on the size of individual loans has been increased from $75,000 to $100,000. This increase is absolutely necessary in view of the steadily growing demand for more and larger loans and in view of inflation. While inflation has hit hard at all of us in the business community, it has hit hardest at the small businessman and businesswoman. These smaller companies, Mr. Speaker, are less able than larger companies to defend themselves and to protect the viability of their companies. In this respect one of the real benefits of this program is that smaller companies can borrow at 1 per cent over prime, a rate which is considerably better than they would be otherwise able to obtain for the purposes which are eligible under the act.
As an additional amendment, Mr. Speaker, a new lending ceiling has been proposed for the two-year period of extension. Whereas the present ceilling will be $675 million for the three-year period ending on June 30, 1980, the new ceiling will be $850 million for the extended two-year period from July 1, 1980, to June 30, 1982. The fact, Mr. Speaker, that the proposed new ceiling is considerably higher than the previous one, even though it will cover a shorter time period, is very clear evidence both of the growing requirement for small business borrowing and the government's willingness to meet this requirement.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the act has been amended to take account of the fact that administration of the program has been transferred from the Department of Finance to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. This transfer is a natural one, as it puts the Small Businesses Loans Act into a department which has a mandate to work closely with and service the needs of small business.

Now that 1 have outlined the major points of Bill C-17, Mr. Speaker, I would like to return briefly to the government's review of financing support programs for small business.
As this House is aware, the government makes available a wide array of financial support for the deserving small business community. For example, the Federal Business Development Bank has been serving the needs of small business since 1944. The bank has established offices all over Canada and at this time has approximately $2 billion in loans outstanding. The FBDB in recent years has also been supplying venture capital to small businesses. In addition to the bank, the enterprise
Small Businesses Loans Act
development program of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce supports a large number of loans to small business and their activity has been furthered by wide decentralization of the program. Last year the program provided approximately $140 million in loan insurance and $90 million in grants.
In addition, financial support is provided to small business through the lower corporate tax rate for smaller firms, and the Department of Regional and Economic Expansion operates financial programs which support small business.
Aside from these federal government initiatives, the provinces have established support programs for small businesses and the private sector has greatly increased its term lending efforts in support of small business, especially in recent years.
In view of all of these activities, the government has undertaken, over the coming months, to review its own programs so that they might better complement other programs, be they provincial or in the private sector.

Indeed, Mr. Speaker, it is the intention of the government during the course of the review to seek the views of the financial community, the small business community and the provincial governments. We expect that such consultation will provide the government with the kind of broadly based advice and analysis which will be necessary to establish the best possible financial support policy for small businesses in the years ahead. Mr. Speaker, this is a vital task. 1 am sure that my predecessor and members of his party as well as my colleagues in the New Democratic Party will also be most willing to advise me on the best ways and means at the disposal of the government to put in place the best programs for small businesses in Canada.
As I said, this is a vital task and it is being done in the knowledge that the health and vitality of the small business sector is of great and lasting importance to the over-all health of the Canadian economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am glad my colleagues had that straightened out because I did not have my notes here regarding Bill C-19. It would have made quite a difference.
I was interrupted at one o'clock at the beginning of my remarks concerning the bill amending the limit and the area of responsibility for the Small Businesses Loans Act. I would like to put on the record a few comments and observations about the act, and perhaps the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe) might take note of these and, in his windup, reply to a question or two.
The Small Businesses Loans Act can, I think, be said to be a very successful program of financial aid to the small business community. As the Minister of State for Small Businesses has said, since it was taken from a ceiling interest rate to a 1 per cent over prime rate, the use of it has expanded dramatically in the private sector.
It has been a very inexpensive program to operate and the losses have never been higher than 0.42 per cent of average loans outstanding. Perhaps it is not generally known to members that the formula virtually removes all risk from the large lenders of these loans in that the government guarantees 95 per cent of the first $125,000 of loans made, 50 per cent of the next $125,000, and 10 per cent of the balance of loans made. This really represents an effective 100 per cent guarantee for the larger lenders.
I am glad to see that the amendment is to bring the dollar ceiling up to something that offsets the deterioration that has taken place in the value of our dollar as a result of the inflationary pressures on our economy.
One of the disappointing things that we might make note of, which the minister might reply to, is the fact that one of the real needs as we study the financial requirements and the changing conditions of the small and medium-sized enterprise sector is working capital. Too often the pressure on working capital or the use of liquidity within the small and mediumsized enterprise units of our economy is for fixed plant or equipment, covering losses, or for unforeseen poor accounts. That is an area where there is serious pressure. I think, when the minister says that the time has come for a total review of the financial needs of the small and medium-sized enterprise sectors, that working capital requirements should be a major part of that review. Also, perhaps the Small Businesses Loans Act might be widened to include working capital in the future. At the moment, working capital is not a part of its terms of reference. We would be wise as members of Parliament representing that important community to have a good look at that as we review this whole matter of financial programs for the business community.
Once again 1 would like to put on the record the importance of the small and medium-sized enterprise sector to the economy and why the review that the Minister of State for Small Businesses mentioned and suggested is so necessary. The small businesses secretariat did a very fine piece of work extracting information from income tax data. On 1,075,000 businesses in Canada, 325,000 were incorporated businesses and 750,000 were unincorporated. Ninety-nine per cent of these businesses have annual sales of less than $2 million; 429,000 of the unincorporated businesses were self-employed professionals.
The total sales of all of the businesses in Canada were $392.2 billion in the year 1976. Of that, the incorporated sector of the business community sold $347.6 million, the unincorporated sector, $44.6 billion. It is interesting to note that 28 per cent of the total sales came from businesses with less than $2 million in annual sales; it is this area which the small business secretariat tries to study and watch over, advising members of Parliament what is needed in that area and which forces for change are coming into play. That is a very important component of our industrial community.
About 225,000 of the unincorporated businesses have sales of less than $10,000 and, believe me, that is within the category of small business. That is what the budget of the former government was trying to do in allowing spouse deductibility in the unincorporated business sector. It would have allowed very considerable relief to that sector. That was an important initiative and I should like to see it carried through.
The business contribution to the gross national product in 1976 was 42 per cent. Thirty per cent of the business compo-
April 25, 1980

nent of the gross national product originated from firms with less than $2 million in annual sales. Fifty-five per cent of the business component of the gross national product originated from firms with less than $20 million in annua! sales. That left government institutions, financial institutions, hospitals and the like, making up 58 per cent of the gross national product. I am putting this on record because it is important we get a feeling which will provide support of the Minister of State for small businesses and to the small business secretariat, and draw attention to a need which hon. members will have to regard with increasing concern.
Within the community 1 have described, total employment amounts to 6.6 million persons according to the 1976 statistics. Businesses with sales of less than $2 million employed 2.5 million people or were responsible for 42 per cent of business employment. Businesses with sales of less than $20 million, which brings us to the small and medium-sized enterprise sector, employed 4.1 million people, or were responsible for 66 per cent of business employment in 1976.
1 put this on record again to outline the impact and the importance of these matters and these instruments and of the study which the Minister of State has told us is part of an ongoing process. It is to that study and to that financial review that I should like to address some remarks. Before doing so, however, there is one other point I wish to raise and 1 would appreciate hearing the minister's remarks with regard to it.
As the small businesses loans legislation has expanded-the minister told us about this in his opening remarks-outside the basic group of chartered banks, and has gone out to include credit unions and other lending institutions, 1 should like the minister to tell us whether he is aware of any change in his liability under this act. I have in mind the nature of the loan, the credit review, the type of institution which is now embraced by the legislation and which has probably opened up a pattern of activity which has not been reflected in practices to date by the larger, more conservative institutions. I, at any rate, would appreciate knowing whether the minister is aware of any change in the minister's liability as a result of the expansion of the program.
The minister told us a financial review was taking place related to all aspects of financial programs affecting the community I have described in my remarks. There is the Small Businesses Loans Act, the act we are amending today; there is the Small Loans Act, an entirely different measure and which perhaps does not touch on the business community other than with regard to accounts receivable. There is the Federal Business Development Bank with regard to which I had the opportunity of explaining my feelings in depth during the debate on Bill C-4 in the Thirty-first Parliament.
1 am sure that the Federal Business Development Bank is sweating it out right now and in need of financial relief in light of the very high cycle of interest rates we are going through. 1 would think that the increasing rate of bankruptcies has been creating a magnitude of change in terms of their liquidity and in terms of pressure upon their accumulated surplus. We would, perhaps, like to be aware of the extent of this pressure.
Small Businesses Loans Act
If the minister could advise as to the change that the last 90 days have brought, and the pressures it has placed upon the Federal Business Development Bank, those of us who are interested would much appreciate the information.
In addition to the extensive work of the Federal Business Development Bank in this field, we have the adjustment assistance programs of the enterprise development under the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. One of the things I found frustrating as minister of state for industry and small businesses in the former government was the magnitude of dollars which my colleague responsible for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion had at his disposal in his dealings with his provincial counterparts, or with industrial counterparts in the provinces, in terms of programs of assistance to the business community. So we have all these different activities going on, different departments all making their play for this audience which is described in the 1976 statistics. If there is one thing which needs co-ordination so as to bring about effectiveness in the use of resources and in the use of the program, it is this area which I have described.
1 am very pleased the minister intends to continue the work in place in the department in bringing about the review of which he spoke. In my view, a basic change of structure is needed to assist the minister because, so far, we in Canada are reacting in what amounts to knee-jerk fashion to political pressures which accompany lobbying by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and so forth.
Now that we have defined the audience and the importance of that audience in the Canadian economy, it behoves both sides of the House to move in on a structure which will serve that community more efficiently and will allow them to use the resources at the disposal of Parliament more effectively. In that review I would like to suggest and submit that perhaps the government should give consideration-or perhaps the minister of state can carry this forward to cabinet-to a standing committee of the House on industry and small business at which the constituency described and now defined could have a platform and a means of communicating with their elected representatives, and particularly with the bureaucracy responsible for the activities and subactivities within the various departments.
Having studied in some detail and debated the proper vehicle through which the industrial community could best be served-or this end of the spectrum of the industrial community-one looks at and studies in some depth the small business act of the United States which has built a massive bureaucracy, put in place programs, has got itself all caught up in definitions within each category, and has indeed become a very cumbersome situation.
If one then moves over into Europe and the European Common Market countries, one will find that the co-ordinating role of the secretariat and the advocacy of the secretariat are being enhanced, but that role in itself can be quite frustrating to the staff within the department. They really do

April 25, 1980
Small Businesses Loans Act
not have the clout that is necessary for the constituency-the statistics I put on the record-really demands and needs. I am sure my colleagues on this side of the House would assist and probably push for a vehicle such as a standing committee on industry and small business which would be able to assist that department and the outside community in co-ordinating the programs and improving the communication between ourselves as elected representatives, members of the business community and the various associations and lobby groups and the bureaucracy, because if there was one thing I found frustrating in the short period in which 1 had the privilege of serving my country as minister of state, it was the difficulty 1 had in moving between departments.
I could get an understanding and a working arrangement going within my area of responsibility, but it was extremely difficult to move that progress through the other departments within the bureaucratic structure, and I think a standing committee of the House would aid immeasurably in the efficient delivery of programs to the business community.
In addition, I am troubled about the ability of the political process, or this process, to communicate the needs and the feelings and the studies from organizations like chambers of commerce, boards of trade, and the various groups which study and gather up the inputs, feelings, wants and wishes of the community. 1 think the struggle that we, as elected representatives, are facing, is the will of the wealth-creating community outside-those people who are engaged in wealth-creating activity and in adding to the value of goods which, after all, create all the payrolls, cash flow and taxes upon which the consolidated revenue fund can finance programs- that the decision-making base be spread more widely where that community can have an incentive to direct its capital and its energies into certain directions.
To me, research and development crystalize the struggle which is going on. I believe the bureaucrats-and 1 speak respectfully when 1 use that term-within two or three departments of government naturally want to keep control unto themselves in terms of research and development, in terms of incentive programs and in terms of venture capital programs, rather than deliver tax points to the community whereby there is an incentive to make a decision to spend a particular block of money in a particular area of risk. That is the debate I would like to see enhanced, and I do not know of what forum it can be developed in other than the standing committee on industry and small business which I am proposing here as a result of the opportunity I had to spend some time studying this area of activity.
Basically the bureaucrat feels that there is more efficiency in delivering research and development incentives through programs than through tax points. I come from that industrial sector out there, and I can tell hon. members that I have not time to come through the paper work and the screening process for those programs, but if 1 had 125 per cent, 1 could have a board of directors' meeting and we could decide that the risk of doing something new that would add to the payrolls and wealth of this country was compensated in that 25 per
cent factor. Then those decisions could be made across the land by the decision makers who, after all, are gambling their own working capital and their own savings, and to me that is an issue which 1 think we have to address, and perhaps we could challenge the desire for programs which many of our friends within the bureaucracy have.
1 think what I have just mentioned is one of the causes of frustration within that industrial community, and I think again-1 am sorry to repeat myself-that such a committee could do much to diffuse that level of frustration and improve the feeling and the spirit of communication between the three forces.
One of the other things that 1 found, I suppose while in office and particularly since being in office, is the lack of awareness that the small business community and the mediumsized enterprise sector have in terms of the government programs which are available, and 1 was going to bring into the House a stack of literature, the ABCs, all of the beautiful literature of the Federal Business Development Bank and the case counselling service, and all of the programs which have to do with each aspect of accounting or procurement in the small business sector.
All of this magnificant material has been put together in very well designed presentations, and yet there is a major lack of awareness within the community. I know that the Federal Business Development Bank has small business seminars. One can see university after university and institution after institution now putting on small business seminars, but the lack of awareness of what is available is another matter I would like to see addressed, and I use the opportunity in this debate on the amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act to make the minister aware that we should again perhaps be in a committee addressing this awareness problem and seeing what can be done to make a more efficient and effective use of the material that is available.
One of the emerging needs in the review on finance that I have seen is the need for risk capital. It is a case now of moving any liquidity over into safer instruments and investments, or giving out some kind of an incentive which protects the high after-tax dollar cost of that type of capital in areas of risk.
I have mentioned working capital, and the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario-and 1 believe B.C. and one of the other provinces; not yet, the minister says-are moving in this area of vehicles for venture capital. There is potential for some abuse there, but I think anything that can move our conservative after tax savings dollars into risk areas of business, with tax shelter protection, would be an initiative that the minister of state could take, and it would have wide and great support from the community at large in Canada.
1 have mentioned research and development policies and programs. We debated extensively through the Thirtieth Parliament, and if the minister cares to look into the files, he will find extensive studies on research and development programs and policies which really have to be delivered to that industrial community if we are going to keep the Canadian industrial
April 25, 1980

plant modern and effective and at highly optimal levels of production efficiency. Too many of the government programs I saw when in office-and which 1 am sure the minister will see-are running after industries which, because of obsolescence, old plant, or emerging technologies in other countries, really cannot compete in the global marketplace.
Tied in with this is the General Agreement on Trades and Tariffs and the phasing out of tariff protection for industries. I suggest that part of that review must be a change in attitude, a change in the use of the government resource from a protective attitude toward industries that are now obsolete in the global market place to delivering programs of front-end benefit and incentive which will allow us to put the highest technology of the world in place within Canada, within the Canadian industrial community, so that we can compete against global efficiency and labour in other parts of the world where there is a lower standard of living and perhaps not the burden of environmental protection that we demand of ourselves.
These are all areas which I do not think this community, through its elected representatives, is debating, and that is one of the reasons why I urge all members of the House to support the call for the establishment of a standing committee on industry and small business where these studies could get wider recognition and more input. Perhaps the combination of programs and tax points could reduce the frustration level which exists, and we could start delivering and creating an awareness of those industrial sectors that need assistance, because that is where the future is and where the payrolls will be tomorrow.
1 am seriously concerned at the extent of the resource that we are delivering in protecting what is obviously obsolete. A classic example, 1 think, is the auto pact crisis which we in this country face today. We knew a decade ago that there had to be product design and product change and that environmental legislation would be coming soon, that we were going to be an energy short continent and that we could not carry on wasting in the way we were. Yet we allowed ourselves to continue blindly building cars with V8 engines, the high horsepower gas burner, while the United States was quietly putting in place the energy-efficient car. Now we have reversed the flow and caused a trade inversion in this country that is of crisis proportion.
If we are going to provide aid to these industrial areas, I think we should provide aid, programs and tax points only in those areas where the product fits the need of the people and of the continent for the decade ahead, where its fits into an energy efficient demand, where we are not protecting that which deserves to be flushed out by the market system, but rather where we are delivering something that can have a market mandate in the global market at large, particularly on the North American continent.
These are some of the problems that I have seen, and now 1 would like to close with one other in the financial area of the SME sector. Much of the Canadian dollar, through our Regis-
Small Businesses Loans Act
tered Retirement Savings Plans, ends up in pension funds in RRSPs, and in the financial institutions which require a secure covenant of safety. There is a financial vehicle that we have been trying to get through three departments of the government, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the insurance branch, and the Department of Finance. There is a vehicle which would allow a covenant to be given to lending institutions which would permit money from those institutions to be fully secured to the lender and yet made available to the business community in amounts of $500,000 to $5 million, in 15 to 30-year terms at interest rates below prime.
As I close my remarks here today, 1 make a plea that the bureaucracy really hear the message because there is a source of funding for the industrial community which lies dormant in these funds and in their security, and which could be made available to the industrial community, relieving the financial pressures which exist if a co-insured first-class covenant could be given to the lending institutions.
One thing that shocks me in the hold up of that vehicle is the fact that the federal government, or its advisers, fails, in its narrow definition of qualified lenders, to take into account such funds as workmen's compensation funds in the provinces, the Alberta Heritage fund, and pension funds from Crown corporations. I think there should be an open mind with regard to them so that that financial resource can be delivered to the industrial community and so that we can get on with building a first-class industrial plant, industries that can compete on an efficient, optimal basis in the global marketplace so that we can truly be ready as a country for the era ahead that the GATT agreement is bringing on us.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise today to speak on the proposed amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act which would raise the ceiling on the amount of money a small business may have outstanding under the act from $75,000 to $100,000, that would increase the amount that may be guaranteed under the act to $850 million, and extend the act for a two-year period until June 30, 1982.
I support this bill with reservations since the benefits accruing to small business under this act have been more than eroded '-.rough the government's monetary policy of maintaining high interest rates in Canada.
Bill C-17 is indeed an insult, not only to the Canadian small businessmen but to Canadians as a whole. It creates the impression that this government is prepared to act and do something for the small business community when, in fact, it is doing very little for Canada's small entrepreneurs. This was misused opportunity, for with this bill the government could have initiated measures which guaranteed to resurrect and build confidence throughout our business community at a time when economic expansion and entrepreneurship are at a very low level indeed. Now we have lost this opportunity to build faith and confidence in our country since the business commu-

April 25, 1980
Small Businesses Loans Act
nity is disappointed and dejected with the contents of this bill. They were expecting so much more.
This bill does nothing to assist the small businessman, and it comes at a time when serious, thoughtful, rational changes are required in our economic structure and in our economic system. In their hearts, Canadians know the present system is inadequate. Canadians know that we are an incredibly rich country with unlimited and unimaginable opportunities, coupled with a young, dynamic, creative and talented people, yet facing such serious problems and difficulties as exist in our country today.
Hon. members to my right, as well as members across the way, tell us that we live in a country committed to the principles of free enterprise and competition. I am afraid this is an illusion, this is a dream. Canadians believe that if an industry is competitive, then we can expect to get a better choice of products in the marketplace and obtain them at lower prices. There exists extensive empirical evidence to support this belief, so long as the conditions for competition do, in fact, exist. However, the reality of the Canadian economy is very different from this competitive model. The key industrial sectors of the Canadian economic system are dominated by a small number of large corporations, and if we recognize that many of these corporations are branch plants of foreign business operations, then we begin to place the structure of the Canadian economy in its appropriate international context.
1 am certain that my colleagues in the House are aware of the extent of corporate concentration in the Canadian economy. No one can look back over the holes left in the economic landscape by the wave of corporate takeovers since the royal commission tabled its report on corporate concentration and fail to realize that our economy is undergoing dramatic and far-reaching structural changes, changes that are not necessarily in the best interests of Canadians.
It is not insignificant that a very key question was left out of the terms of reference of the Royal Commission on Corporate Concentration. That key question is: how has federal government policy contributed to and accelerated the process of corporate concentration in Canada? Or, to put it another way, how has the federal government contributed to the erosion of competitive enterprise in this country and as a result placed many small businessmen in an unfair competitive position?
Is it any wonder that, for decades, big business, and often foreign business, has exercised undue influence on the formation of economic policy in Canada? The current economic crisis has brought this to the attention of all Canadians, but to none more forcefully than those employed in small business. For it is here, in the small business sector, that the conditions for competition exist and the competitive forces of the market place have their greatest impact. For decades the government has ignored this vital sector of our economy. Only last year it finally got around to publishing its First major statistical
review of small business. Using the criteria of sales less than $2 million to define small and more than $20 million to define big, the following picture of business in Canada emerged. I should like to refer to a few specific points in that review.
In 1976 there were 628,000 small businesses in Canada representing 97 per cent of all businesses. The 2,000 largest businesses in Canada represent less than one half of 1 per cent of all businesses. Small businesses account for nearly 28 per cent of total business sales. In terms of employment, small businesses account for approximately 40 per cent of the Canadian labour force.
A recent study by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business indicates that small businesses have created more than 50 per cent of new jobs outside the government sector since 1971. But small business is vital to the Canadian economy for other reasons. While 48 per cent of big business in Canada is foreign-owned, over 96 per cent of small business is Canadian-owned. I emphasize Canadian-owned and Canadian-operated. Small business in Canada is an expression of the Canadian character, and extension of Canada's energetic and imaginative people, representing their hopes, dreams, aspirations and concerns for the future.
The decision to go into business in Canada is a decision to take one's future into one's own hands. It involves risk, frustration, and great deal of hard work. When we talk of small business in Canada, certainly we are not talking about a faceless and soulless corporation, but indeed of people. Small business is a people business, and we must do everything possible to nurture, encourage and support it.
Small business has been hit especially hard in the present economic crisis. The uncertainties associated with the 1970s have contributed to a marked increase in the number of business failures. Commercial bankruptcies in the first two months of 1980 were up nearly 25 per cent over the same period last year. Bankruptcy experts estimate that at least 75 per cent of failures occur among small businesses. Just this afternoon I had the opportunity over lunch to meet with two visiting businessmen from my own riding. One businessman owned a small clothing store and the other businessman represented a small contracting firm. Both of these individuals are on the brink of bankruptcy. The high interest rates, and the monetary policy which is perpetuated and supported by the present government, have driven these entrepreneurs to the edge.
In the face of the current downturn, this bill to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act betrays a colossal failure on the part of the government. It will do virtually nothing to ease the burden on small businesses in Canada. The increase in the loan ceiling from $75,000 to $100,000 proposed in this bill, once one takes into account the inflation over the past three years, represents no increase at all in real borrowing power. In 1979 less than 3 per cent of the value of all small business loans were guaranteed under the Small Businesses Loans Act. There are a number of reasons for this which the legislation does not even begin to address.
April 25, 1980

For example, guaranteed loans can only be used for purchase or expansion of plant, equipment or land. Loans cannot be used to provide working capital which, of course, is one of the most important capital requirements of the small businessman, the small entrepreneur. The final decision to extend a loan rests by and large with Canadian chartered banks. They have been reluctant to use this act because of the limits placed on the interest that can be charged. Why charge prime plus 1 per cent if one can get prime plus 3 per cent? In fact the chartered banks have a vested interest in not supporting this program throughout the land.
Small businesses have indicated that branch managers in the chartered banks and other lending agencies are either reluctant to talk about the Small Businesses Loans Act or are not familiar with the program, or at least they say that they are not familiar with it. The one exception to this is the heavier use of the plan by the Banque Canadienne Nationale in Quebec. We hope the minister has received commitments from the chartered banks and other lending agencies that they will actively participate in the small business loans program, and if he has not received such a commitment, we hope that he actively seeks one.
Also I feel it is important to point out that less than $500 million will be available under the Small Businesses Loans Act each year. In fact this is only a small fraction of the $9 billion borrowed by small businesses in the year 1979. As one of my hon. colleagues mentioned previously, it does not address one of the serious problems facing entrepreneurs, that is, the lack of information. Some method must be found to enable potential investors or businessmen to be more aware of the existing 400 programs of interest to them.
The real failure to provide leadership, not only in the area of small business but to the Canadian economy as a whole, is the shortsighted and misguided monetary policy which has left small business and the economy in general saddled with record-high interest rates. When the prime interest rate is 16.75 per cent, the few benefits provided by the Small Businesses Loans Act cease to be meaningful.
Short-term, simplistic, cosmetic legislation such as the Small Businesses Loans Act which we are debating today would not be needed if the government had, in the past, provided responsible leadership in implementing a sound longterm industrial strategy for Canada. High interest rates, a record balance of payments deficit, and an unprecedented federal government deficit, all point to a colossal failure to fulfil the public trust.
In travelling about the country I have had the opportunity to speak with large and small groups of businessmen about the problems which they are currently facing. I hope the hon. minister and his government will be introducing legislation during this session which will address some of the serious problems mentioned previously in this discussion.
I have yet to discuss and examine the throttling impact that government red tape has on the small businessman. The paper
Small Businesses Loans Act
requirements of the federal government have placed the small businessman in a very difficult position and have resulted in undue stress and frustration, as well as placing added personnel costs on his accounts book. Also 1 should like to remind the minister that at present a corporate tax system exists which treats small businesses differently than large businesses. The present tax system actually discriminates against small business by imposing higher effective tax rates on small businesses than on larger corporations.
In closing, I feel compelled to relate to this House an incident which occurred in my riding of Kamloops-Shuswap during the last election campaign. During that campaign I emphasized the fact that, of the three federal political parties, only one consistently and actively supports the concept of fair and equitable individual enterprise and fair and free individual initiative in the marketplace. I suggest that party is the New Democratic Party.
