speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members, it is certainly my pleasure to speak to Bill C-17, an act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, which has been brought forward by my colleague, the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe). The minister has outlined the details of Bill C-17, and he has also briefly outlined the general purposes and the history of the Small Businesses Loans Act. In addition, he has outlined the government's intention to work with the financial community, the small business community and the provincial governments in preparing a complete review of the government's financial support programs for small businesses.
I should like to commend the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) for his constructive remarks in relation to this review and to the amendments to the act presented here today.
I would like to refer ever so briefly to comments of the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), and refer specifically to the drop in interest rates that took place for the last two consecutive weeks since the opening of this Thirty-second Parliament. 1 feel this reflects confidence in the government and it is an indicator that the proposals outlined in the Speech from the Throne are quite proper and correct.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
In speaking to Bill C-17 1 would like to add some comments on the coverage provided by the program. The Minister of State for Small Businesses has already referred to

April 25, 1980
Small Businesses Loans Act
the broad national impact of the program as witnessed by its regional coverage and the very wide and growing participation by a variety of financial institutions.
In addition to this coverage, a broad range of types of businesses are supported through the Small Businesses Loans Act. 1 submit at this time that this is an act that covers all of Canada, whether it be the small towns and villages in the rural sector or the small businesses in the cities across this nation. It is vital to the sustenance of the small business community from coast to coast.
Statistics for 1978 show, for example, that of the total value of loans in that year, wholesale trade accounted for 4.1 per cent, transportation accounted for 8.6 per cent, construction accounted for 9.9 per cent, manufacturing accounted for 14 per cent, retail trade accounted for 26.6 per cent, and service businesses accounted for 35.9 per cent.
It can be seen that the Small Businesses Loans Act provides broad coverage of types of businesses, many of which are traditionally in the small business category. It does not include two additional types of small businesses, farming and fisheries, but they are supported by two other special federal government programs; first of all under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and secondly, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. As announced in the Speech from the Throne, both of these acts will also be brought forward for renewed consideration by the government in the very near future.
In the course of presentation of Bill C-17 I think it is important to note the philosophy which underpins not only the Small Businesses Loans Act but also all the other federal government debt-financing programs.
A basic premise behind all federal government debt-financing programs is that they should complement rather than compete with private sources of loan capital. This is more than just a philosophical stance in respect of the roles of the private and public sectors. It is based on the realization that the government can be most effective by working with the private financial institutions to make better use of the very extensive delivery systems that are already in place in the private sector. For this reason, the success of the Small Businesses Loans Act should be measured not only in terms of the volume of business undertaken, but also, and perhaps just as important, in terms of its success in stimulating private lenders to expand both the form and volume of financing to small businesses.
The Small Businesses Loans Act is in keeping with this philosophy. It is a program which has been administered effectively with as little government involvement as is possible. All of the transactions between borrowers and lenders takes place within the private sector with the government acting only as a guarantor.
We all know that this cannot always be the case, but there are good reasons behind the government which has also established direct lending and grant programs. The programs have been established to meet special circumstances which face Canada's ever-growing businesses. Even where direct lending programs are in effect, however, an attempt is made, if at all
possible, to involve private lenders as co-financiers. This is as it should be, Mr. Speaker, and I think the small businessmen and small business women of this country would agree with me. They do not want handouts from the government. They want, and only when it is necessary, a boost from the government to assist them in their own efforts to build the businesses. They want to retain their independence and to go about their business as they see fit. The Small Businesses Loans Act is a program which follows this approach.
In concluding my brief remarks on this Small Businesses Loans Act I want to re-emphasize that this program is an important source of financing for small businesses. It provides suppport to thousands of deserving men and women who run businesses which are the backbone of our Canadian economy. I take great pleasure, therefore, in having spoken to this bill.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had to speak in the House since it reconvened and I should like to convey to you, sir, my congratulations on your appointment, and ask you to convey to your colleagues, especially Madam Speaker, my best wishes on the duties they have undertaken in this House. I know that all of you will serve the House well. You are all experienced in the operations of the House and we look forward with great pleasure to working with you.
Let me now say a few words about this bill. The small business sector, as we know it, is the largest employer in Canada of our labour force, employing some 6.6 million people. It is something that governments at all levels talk about, federal, provincial and municipal. It is the most difficult area for the federal people to really get involved with because so many of these businesses fall under provincial jurisdiction. When it comes down to it, I suppose it is really the role of the federal government to create an atmosphere in which that small business enterprise can flourish.
I am not that familiar with the new minister of small businesses, and I do not know his background or whether or not he was ever a small businessman. This bill may encourage him to become one in the near future. I feel that the former minister during our government, my colleague, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), was probably the first minister, at least since I have been present in this House, who knew what it was to be a small businessman because he has been one for a number of years. The hon. member for Capilano knows what it is like to go out and raise capital, employ people, and to design and devise a product which will sell and earn a profit.
If the present minister of small businesses does not have any business experience, then I hope that he is a good listener because there is much to learn from the small business community, and indeed from the members of this House. As I say, perhaps the minister will be encouraged at some future point to enter the field of business. It is a very fascinating endeavour to undertake.
April 25, 1980

As the hon. member for Capilano has just said, the problems which the small businessman must face are, to some extent, helped by this bill. One of the major problems that I found with the Small Businesses Loans Act when I have had to deal with it over the past eight years was that most people are of the false belief that the federal government lends the money. They do not understand. It would be a good idea to put out some publicity indicating that the government does not lend the money, but merely guarantees a loan through the bank. But that is an area I will cover in a moment.
Another thing which many people do not understand about the Small Businesses Loans Act is the interest rate which has had a series of strange manipulations over the years. As I recall the original act the rate of interest was 6 per cent. At that time the bank interest rate was 7.5 per cent. Obviously the banks were not interested in loaning money under this act at the lower rate. The bank rate increased to 8 per cent and 9 per cent while the small business loans rate remained at 6 per cent. Then the interest rate under the act changed. I believe that the rate was determined by the yield on a selected series of government bonds which was altered biannually in April and October.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: Semi-annually.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
At any rate, it was twice a year. However, the bond market dropped, and of course the rate of return on the bonds dropped, leaving the interest rate on small business loans in the same mess that it was in before. At this time hon. members would rise in the House during question period or during speeches and ask the minister of finance, who was John Turner, I believe, why the small businessmen were not able to get a loan under the Small Businesses Loans Act and why the banks were playing games with the small businessmen. When these small businessmen would say to the banks, "I would like to borrow some money under the Small Businesses Loans Act", the bank accountant would say, "I've never heard of it". Mr. Turner would answer, "I'm having lunch tomorrow or next week with the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association. I will bring the matter up, and we will see what we can do". Of course, nothing ever happened.
This charade went on year after year, and to some extent is still going on today. In fact the banks at one time, in order to keep the Minister of Finance off their backs for not lending money under the Small Businesses Loans Act, were using the act as a form of a gift to their better accounts. The banks were not helping the small entrepreneur who had a venture capital problem and needed assistance. They were giving loans under the act to their good accounts which paid their bills regularly, kept up their deposits, and had a good record with the bank. In other words, they were using it as a plumb.
The banks would say to these good accounts who were interested in expanding their business under the Small Businesses Loans Act, "Yes, we will get the loan for you because the rate is lower than what we charge on our normal commercial accounts, which will be of some advantage to you". These banks should have been loaning money to businessmen who did
Small Businesses Loans Act
not have the necessary collateral to obtain the money in the private sector. For the most part, that charade has disappeared.
I would recommend that the minister speak to the officials of his department and, while I do not like to see more paper, recommend that a pamphlet be printed. It could be entitled, "How to get a loan under the Small Businesses Loans Act". The Minister of Finance should lean a little more on the chartered banks and insist that they display these pamphlets on the counters of the branches across the country. This would help a great deal.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: Put the minister's picture on it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: When this bill gets to the committee of the whole stage, standing committee, or wherever it is to go, I intend to introduce amendments which cover areas of some concern to me. I am a small businessman, so I know the problems.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: Did you say small?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
I will get you for that!
I would like to see an amendment which will allow loans under this act to be used for working capital. I would like to see provision within the act to allow for loans to be used to complete research and development projects. Let me expand on that topic for a moment. I have been in and out of big business, small business, and I have worked for multinationals, conglomerates, and I now have my own business. I know what it is all about. The person who turns off the research and development project in a small business is not the engineer or development man but the comptroller, the guy who controls the cheque book. He or she is the one who turns off the cash flow because there are just not enough funds to complete the project.
Most innovations and most of the patents are made by people in the small business field. There should be an amendment in the act to allow for the completion of research and development projects. I would be fair and say that the applicant would have to prove that the amount of money being loaned would in fact complete the project.
The third amendment which I intend to move would allow the Small Businesses Loans Act to register patents on a product, process or device developed in the small business field. Many times a small businessman expends all his money developing a device, process or product, only to find that he needs a good deal more money to register the patent in Canada, the United States, Great Britain, or any country where he wishes to protect his product.
The Small Businesses Loans Act could be used in the acquisition of a patented process, product or device to be used by a small business. The way the market is going today and particularly considering the volatility of foreign exchange, one finds that some in the small business community are in a

April 25, 1980
Small Businesses Loans Act
position to license a product which they are presently importing. This helps their balance of payments problem and helps to develop the whole entrepreneurial level of small business.
If the minister would like to introduce these three amendments, I would be happy to convey them to him for introduction, as long as it is done. That is all 1 am interested in. Something must be done.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), when he was chairman of the finance committee in a previous parliament, and I went through the Bank Act. I am sure that he will recall section 88 of that act which deals with accepting as collateral raw materials and work in progress. At our in camera committee meeting where we were dealing with the inspector general of banks, we agreed to amend that section of the Bank Act, especially for the small businessman. We felt they should be able to offer their inventories as collateral. I know the minister recalls this because we had a long conversation with the inspector general of banks. He and 1 finally saw eye to eye and had the act amended. That is the bill that will now come before this House and we appreciate that, because it is going to help the small businessman.
It is the small businesses that employ the bulk of the labour force in this country and contribute the largest amount of the gross national product that is the stabilizer in our economy. When you look at the labour involvement in the small business community at large, you find that they rarely lay people off. Even if the economy turns down, they keep them on because of the difficulties they have in getting and retaining people. One of the ways they retain staff is not to lay them off as some of the larger companies do, when the economy turns down. By adopting that sort of principle or philosophy or strategy-call it what you will-they impart a great deal of stability to our economy. If we can do anything to assist them, Mr. Speaker, and to expand this sector, we will help the economy to flourish and move ahead.
There has been mention of the amount of paper that small businessmen have to deal with. I recall that a previous minister in the small business portfolio of an earlier Parliament set up a committee to examine the problems of the small businessman in dealing with all this paper. I should like to tell you something of the practical difficulties that I faced when I was in business because of the amount of paper that came in. We used to separate the paper into two piles-that from Statistics Canada was piled on one side of the table and that from Revenue Canada was piled on the other side. We knew that we had to pay our taxes, so we always looked after the pile from Revenue Canada. The other pile grew higher and higher and we started getting threatening phone calls from some clerk in Statistics Canada. It became a serious matter for us. With only a small staff, we had to ask ourselves whether we were going out to do some business, to design something, fabricate something, sell something-or were we going to sit down and fill out all these forms, some of which were totally irrelevant to our operation.
I am a very practical person, Mr. Speaker, and I was determined to find a solution to the problem. One day up town I went into a rubber stamp shop and bought a large rubber stamp which said "Not Applicable." I also bought a red stamp pad. Back at the office I stamped this great pile of government forms with "Not Applicable" and sent them all back to Statistics Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
In return I received a computerized letter which said something to the effect that "we are in receipt of flip-flip, your communication on form so and so which we understand is flip-flip not applicable." We duly filed this in our folder and when the repeat form came in we stamped it "not applicable", made a copy of the letter from Statistics Canada and sent it back to them. Mr. Speaker, we cut our paper load by 66 per cent.
I would recommend that to anyone as a method of cutting down on the paper work that comes across his desk from government. Much of it is just so much nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: Would you change?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
No, I would not change.
Let me move into another area of operation for small businesses, Mr. Speaker. One of the difficulties that small businessmen in this country face is the constant change in the method by which their products are distributed throughout North America. The United States is our largest supplier and we are their largest customer, so there is a tremendous amount of trade back and forth. That applies to Europe to some extent as well.
A series of events have occurred in North America, starting with the imposition of the 10 per cent surcharge that President Nixon put on imports to the United States when that country was having a balance of payments problem. Following that, the United States established DISC, the Domestic International Sales Corporation, the purpose of which was to entice American companies operating overseas to return to the United States, produce their goods there, and then export them.
One of the provisions of the DISC program was that 50 per cent of the profit may be retained by business, tax free, at the pleasure of the president. That meant that the profit on a great deal of export dollars was retained in the business-tax free at the pleasure of the president. Mr. Speaker, I do not know that any president is going to have the courage to rescind that! The program has had a dramatic effect on the conduct of commerce in the small and medium-sized business sector of this country. It has changed the whole method of distribution. In the past a manufacturer built a product, put it in inventory and then shipped from inventory. That is not done today. Now a product comes off the production line and is shipped immediately to the downstream distribution system. This has taken the cost of carrying inventory from the manufacturer and passed it on to the wholesaler and the retailer. The difficulty
April 25, 1980

with this is that in this country our financial system has not responded, and the effect is felt by the small and medium-sized businessses.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I say to the minister, through you, that I want to see this Small Businesses Loans Act amended to ensure that the funds that are acquired may be used for working capital.
Earlier I mentioned section 88 of the Bank Act which will become section 177 of the new act. It will help as well, because at the present time a small retailer like the one mentioned by an hon. member opposite, a clothing retailer in the throes of bankruptcy, has to pay for his merchandise when he receives it. If he offers it to the bank as collateral, he will only get 30 per cent of its value because the bank will take it under a floating charge. The result is that he is only getting 30 per cent of the value of an asset when it is offered to the bank as collateral.
Through this change in the act we hope that we can help in such cases by having a greater proportion of the value of finished inventory accepted as collateral by the banks so that the small businessman could pay his bills and stay in business.
The record of bankruptcies between 1968 and 1979 is absolutely staggering-the number more than doubled, and 1 suppose by the end of 1980 it will have tripled. These were all little manufacturing concerns, Mr. Speaker, and the major reason for them going under was the lack of working capital. Someone goes into business, mortgages his house, his cottage, his car, his wife-everything-

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: His mother-in-law?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: His mother-in-law-anything the bank will take.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: How much would he get for his mother-in-law?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
That depends! At any rate, he mortgages anything he can to get his business going. Once he does, he thinks it is great and that he is really going to make some money. He gets a large number of orders, but then he has no working capital. That is exactly what happens. You have people who have the initiative to start something, to design something, and to invent something. They get their business going and then run out of funds. What do these people do? They sell out, maybe to their competitor, or they tough it out and go bankrupt. A few of them that are wily enough shake the surface and manage to succeed. So we have to find a series of ways to help this small business sector. Part of this help is here before us.
I commend the minister for introducing this bill. I am not opposed to the Small Businesses Loans Act coming under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray). In fact I think that is a step forward and a good thing. Considering when it came under the jurisdiction of the minister of finance, if past experience is any criterion. The
Small Businesses Loans Ari
businessman will get a better shake from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce than he ever would from the Minister of Finance. At least we will not have to rely on the Minister of Finance having lunch with the chairman of the Canadian Bankers' Association and asking him, "Charlie, can't you help those little guys?". To which Charlie replies, "Well, we are up to the limit of the amount of money we can lend, Mr. Minister. We have done about everything we can", and the thing just falls apart.
One of the great things about our economy is that it is resilient. A lot of that resiliency is in the small business sector. While there is a lot of doom and gloom around, I am not at all pessimistic about the future. I have a great deal of confidence in the business community, and in the small business sector particularly. But these people do need help. They need it now, and they are going to need it for some period of time.
I can only ask the minister to take these remarks into consideration, to give whatever aid and assistance we can to these people, and even if he is not a small businessman himself, as long as he is prepared to listen and take the advice of others, I am sure he will do well in his portfolio.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Weatherhead (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity today to say a few words in support of Bill C-17, an act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act. I am even more pleased to say a few words on behalf of small business in general.
First, I would like to remind the House that it was our government in a previous Parliament-1 believe it was the Thirtieth Parliament-that brought in this very important ministry, the Ministry of State for Small Business.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
Frankly, I think the setting up of this ministry was long overdue at that time, but at least around 1977 the government at that time did bring in this ministry to look at the specific interests of small businesses.
1 would also like to congratulate the present Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe), and to wish him well in his new portfolio.
I listened with interest to comments of members opposite and, of course, to what the parliamentary secretary had to say. I believe that there is no question the former minister, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), is well known for his commitment to small business in Canada. I believe his comments and suggestions will be well taken by the minister.
I thought the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) perhaps ranged a bit far in some of his comments, but when he was talking about the importance of Canadian small businessmen I agreed with him wholeheartedly.
The hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) made his comments based on suggestions with respect to possible amendments-while it is not up to me to say whether the amendments might be in order on this particular fairly limited

April 25, 1980
Sinall Businesses Loans Act
type of bill that is before us as far as amending the present bill is concerned-and with regard to the need to look at some of these matters to help small business, and these are well taken and should be considered further.
There is no question that small business, as other speakers have said today, is the life-blood of the Canadian economy. These are the people who make the Canadian economy tick.
1 see by my notes that Canadian small business employs more than 2.5 million people representing 40 per cent of the work force in the private sector. However, 1 remember that the hon. member for Burlington talked in terms of over six million people. But 1 believe that if we are really talking about 2.5 million it must be because of a very narrow definition of small business, because surely Canadian small business really takes in the bulk of the work force in Canada in one way or another.
A healthy small business community in Canada is the best way that there is to ensure more employment in Canada. These are the people who can and do employ more people when times are good and things are expanding. Therefore we must do everything possible to encourage small business in every way.
in my own borough of Scarborough in eastern Toronto, small business employs most of the people in this borough which has 400,000 people. There are a few big businesses but almost all business in Scarborough is small business of various sizes. New small businesses have been encouraged in recent years in the Scarborough area, particularly by the municipal government. This has been especially so under the leadership of the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) who was mayor of Scarborough during most of the 1970s. However, the financial well-being of small businesses depends very heavily on the economic and fiscal climates of Canada as a whole, as well as particular pieces of legislation that can make financial life a bit easier for Canadian small business.
Bill C-17 is an amendment of one such necessary piece of legislation that will help Canadian small businesses.
We heard from the minister earlier today that the program has been a highly successful one which has been in place since 1961, and it is now quite well accepted by the Canadian financial community.
Private financial markets are doing most of the job in lending the money to small businesses for long-term financing, with automatic federal guarantees on eligible loans. We have heard that since the program started over $1 billion in loans has been guaranteed. Last year alone some $250 million worth of loans was guaranteed.
We have heard the details of the amending bill, the fact that it extends the act for two years, and that the limit to a borrower is being raised to $100,000 and that the aggregate amount of guaranteed loans for the period ending June 30, 1980, has been increased to $675 million. The act also proposes that for the next two-year period to June 30, 1980, a maximum of $850 million be guaranteed.
The jurisdiction changes from being under the Minister of Finance to that of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce as far as the main minister is concerned.
I would like to note that extensive review of the financial support programs for small business will be undertaken during the next two years. For example, the programs of the Federal Business Development Bank, the enterprise development fund, and Small Loans Act, which the minister referred to briefly this morning and outlined some of the benefits, will be reviewed. This review may require some substantial amendments at that time as conditions change and opportunities develop in this important sector of our community.
I believe that this review, which the minister undertook this morning and which has been commented on extensively, particularly by the hon. member for Capilano, is probably the most important part of the minister's comments, if I may say so. It is essential, in my view, that the programs of the Federal Business Development Bank, the enterprise development fund and the Small Loans Act be strongly and critically reviewed, and that amendments be proposed, and also that new legislation should be introduced which will make those programs more beneficial and useful for this most important part of the Canadian economy, Canadian small business.
Hon; Alvin Hamilton (Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain): Mr. Speaker, I am no expert on the details of small business but I do have a great interest in doing everything possible to help small business in Canada carry the load it is presently bearing.
It is not a new principle that loans guaranteed by government should be advanced to private business. The best example of precedent for this type of legislation is the Farm Improvement Loans Act introduced some 30 years ago which did so much to help farmers improve the efficiency of their operations and increase their incomes as well. In the course of its application, even the banks learned something about agriculture; some bank managers become very proficient and were most helpful to their farm clients.
I am not here to speak against the principle of this legislation. What I am here to do is to suggest the rock upon which it is going to collapse. This rock has been there for many months but we, at this moment in our history as parliamentarians, should see where the danger lies and take the necessary steps to avoid it. My proposals will not require any amendment to the legislation. They will simply require the minister to take power under the regulations and, in arranging the interest rates, to do the things which are necessary to avoid the pitfalls which exist at this moment in monetary and fiscal policy in Canada.
It is obvious I am referring to the fact that we are at a mad moment of economic history in the western world. All the countries in the western world find themselves under the firm control of people advocating monetary philosophy and principles that in fact are wrong. What they learned in school 30 or 40 years ago does not apply to the type of economy we see today in the western industrial world. Without going into a
April 25, 1980

long lecture on this subject I say flatly that every person in this Parliament understands what I am talking about. Last fall we had the ridiculous spectacle in Canada of the Bank of Canada raising interest rates sharply on the grounds that the Americans were raising their interest rates. The Germans are now doing it, so are the Dutch, the Swiss and the Japanese.
We are all in a period of international monetary madness which every single person of common sense in every country knows is madness. It is not enough for us to make that generalized statement. What we have to do as parliamentarians is to use one quality we possess-a quality these brilliant theoretical people of a generation ago are ignoring. And that is common sense. Every one of us can stand up in this House and give horror story after horror story of what has happened to individuals who were called small businessmen-and that includes farmers-in their own constituencies. The rock which has smashed these promising, enterprising businesses has been these unrealistic, highly dangerous interest rates. And all because of a fallacious theory.
A number of hon. members in this chamber sat with us on the finance committee when we questioned the governor of the Bank of Canada and the minister of finance. Those who were present will recall that the governor admitted that the three reasons he had given for following the Americans were not borne out by quantitative evidence. I asked him whether he had the evidence after two years of raising interest rates following the American pattern, that his policy was working, and in each case the record shows that he said no. He was flying by the seat of his pants in heavy clouds with hard, rocky mountains in the clouds. He was trying to direct the plane of monetary policy in a very dangerous situation.
For example, one of the fears of these brilliant minds who guide our destinies in the monetary and fiscal fields in Canada, is that if the dollar drops in value by 1 per cent this will cause increased costs to those in Canada who buy imported goods. That is true. When I questioned the third-last minister of finance-they come pretty fast in this House, as you know, Mr. Speaker-he told us that for every 1 per cent by which the dollar dropped, the cost to people across Canada would probably be one-quarter of I per cent. One-quarter of 1 per cent of what? We import about $50 billion worth of goods a year. I cannot work with quarters; it is beyond my mental capacity. Take the figure of 1 per cent, four times greater than the minister of finance mentioned.
If the dollar drops I per cent on $50 billion of imported goods it costs all the people of Canada an extra $500 million every year. That is the inflationary lift, cost-push. When I asked the governor of the Bank of Canada what was the total amount of money out on fixed terms of interest in Canada he very kindly sent me a letter containing all the figures. Over $500 billion at any given moment in Canada is out at fixed terms of interest-like this loan will be at under the amendment we are considering. Add 1 per cent to that rate across that whole body of debt and you add $5 billion a year to the cost to all the people of Canada-$5 billion as opposed to half a billion, which is ten times more by trying to fight inflation by
Small Businesses Loans Act
monkeying around with the Canadian dollar than it would be by forcing interest rates up.
Every parliamentarian can take that easy figure, half a billion versus five billion, and so the enormity of what this crazy madness has done to our western countries, particularly the United States and Canada, this last two years is there for all to figure out. Interest rates have literally gone from 7 per cent and 8 per cent to way over 16 per cent and 17 per cent. When we realize what that does as we change our financial instruments-mortgages are a prime example-up to higher rates and when it spreads through the system, we have added to the cost of living and the cost of producing, many billions of dollars in a single year. I use the word "madness" because that is the mildest word I can think of to describe it.
I am not going to continue talking about the gloom and doom effect that this will cause us all. 1 simply want to find positive, simple and constructive ways of avoiding it. Let us make up our minds that it is no fault of the governor of the Bank of Canada that he is following this theory, because every economist in the whole western world is doing it. God is in his heaven, and Keynes is right there beside him.
The reality is that we are destroying the country. We are destroying the United States, Canada and the western world, not to mention the newly developing nations. Therefore, let us get down to what our job is.
1 am not going to talk about the money supply. I think the bank governor is doing a fairly satisfactory job in bringing down the snake. I am not going to talk about the lack of co-operation, co-operating that should have been there for the last thirty years between the central bank, ministers of finance and the great commercial banks. The hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) gave an example of why there has to be that co-operation. I am not going to talk about that.
What is one simple thing that we can do under this legislation, without amending it, which will get away from this danger? On the assumption that we all agree that interest rates are the most dangerous part of the inflationary package, how can we get them down and still be economic and still not subsidize? There is nothing new in this idea that 1 am going to propose. It is as old as the system of money itself. If we look at the business sections of newspapers from this last year, almost every week we see some large corporation announcing it is going to issue a tremendous amount of equity.
Massey-Ferguson talks about putting $500 million of equity on the market. Noranda used that device to fight takeovers. They use this money they get in from equity to pay off this fixed rate of return on interest charges and get down their costs. They gamble, rightly, that every individual in the country who is interested in saving money or investing, knows that a person who has invested in a bond or any type of financial instrument with the same fixed return on it has lost money in the last ten-year inflationary period. They know that he is willing to gamble on putting his money into a type of instrument, equity, which has no guaranteed return, as a rule. He

April 25, 1980
Small Businesses Loans Act
will gamble that that company can save itself, and he will get more money out of the dividends that accrue to him inlater years. Because we see big companies saving themselves this way gives us the clue of how we can do it for small business.
Small business, as a rule, is not set up at this moment in a public company form or even a private company form, for they can go out and issue equity and change the amounts from time to time. However, under this legislation there is a way of doing it, and that is to suggest that the interest rate you are going to charge is, say, 8 per cent. I pick the figure of 8 per cent out of the air. It is very close to the amount of interest that is available to the same small businessman under this development bond concept which was put forward in the Crosbie budget and was renewed by the minister the other day in the mini-budget, where you can call your loan a development bond on which you do not pay interest. You pay dividends, and you take advantage of the loophole in our tax techniques. The banks say, "If you borrow under this provision, since we do not have to pay tax on that type of income, we will give you the interest rate at about half the average interest rate". That is my layman's understanding of how the development bond concept works.
I am simply saying-that is still going to go forward, as 1 understand the mini-budget-why not make this roughly the same? If the average interest rate under the development bond concept is now 7.5 per cent or 8 per cent, let us make it 8 per cent for the small businessman in this legislation. The immediate reaction I get is that that is subsidy and that I am asking the government to go out and borrow money at 15 per cent and 16 per cent and lend it at 8 per cent. My answer is very simple. You say you are going to lend the money at 8 per cent, but you are going to have a faster pay-out with this lower interest amount, and then after the debt is paid off you want a percentage of the profit for "X" number of years.
When you put that up to the lender and you put your hypothetical cash flow chart for the next ten or 15 years in front of him and he sees that this loan of $100,000 is going to add, say, $20,000 a year to your profit picture, even though there is a negative cash flow in the early period, if he can get that debt paid off quickly at 8 per cent and get his money back to re-invest and then have this 2 per cent, 3 per cent, 4 per cent, 5 per cent-even up to 10 per cent, depending on the situation-of the new profit, he can figure it out over a 20-year period that he is going to make more money this way than the other way. The borrower is better off. He does not have a heavy front-end loading during the period of negative cash flow. The lender is going to make more money. There is no subsidy by the government. The guy feels independent. It is a straight business deal.
That type of proposal is not new. 1 have suggested in the committee that we should use it for Farm Credit Corporation loans. All the regulations are there to allow for it. I have suggested we use it for export business, which takes a longer period of time before you get a cash flow in, and the walking money period is three years, four years, and sometimes five years.
1 have suggested it should also apply to the buying of homes. There is not much use in using the word "profit" when buying a home, but let us just change the word "profit" to "capital gains". You will lend the money to a man on a home at 6 per cent. Then you say, "If you sell that home in ten years and make any capital gain, we want half of it". All of a sudden they get their pencils out and the fellow realizes he can afford to buy the home at 6 per cent. The other fellow takes his pencil out. He knows what the figures are. He knows that 80 per cent of all new homes built in Canada and the United States in the last ten or 15 years change hands in ten years. He just plays the average. He knows the capital gains. They go up and down. Whatever figure you take-make it 8 per cent for the loan for the house and a quarter of the capital gain-you can show mathematically that both people are better off.
This is not a new type of thinking. I have seen it being done in business. 1 told several of my friends last fall that I talked this way to a group of businessmen who wanted to lend money in Canada, and I suggested there was not much point in lending money at 14 per cent because you put such heavy front-end loading onto this business that they never get up and get the product these people want. They asked what I would propose. I said, "Well, make it 8 per cent." I said, "Go back and work out your cash flow charts. You know the costs. You know the value of the product because that is in the contract. You know the length of the contract. See what you propose". 1 said, "make it 8 per cent, pay off the debt faster, get a share of the profits, and you will be better off." They came back in two months, the deal was signed and was in the headlines of all the Vancouver newspapers. It amounted to $30 million at 5 per cent. This was not 20 years ago, it was last fall.
You lend money not because you worship the rate. You lend money to make money. If you make more money at 5 per cent and a share of the profit, that is where you go. There is this worship of the fixed type of finance instrument in every type of business we do that has developed in the last ten or 15 years in the western countries, and they call it leverage, etc. If interest rates are low, it is advantageous to borrow the biggest proportion of your capital and operating needs. But now that the interest rates are no longer at that level, it is certainly destructive to business. I say that at their present level it is suicidal to the great majority of big business and little business alike.
I think I have said enough to make my point clear. 1 have suggested that this can be applied to other legislation we have already on the books. 1 am certain that if we think really hard, we could find other examples where we could apply the same principle where you still have the guarantee to the bank, where you still have the concept of trying to get money into the hands of those who do not have all the types of assets that most lending institutions want. I want to suggest that credit unions and banks will be forced by competition to go into this type of practice, as well as the governments.
Every one of us, I know, has read the reports of the Economic Council of Canada. They put out last fall their major report
April 25, 1980

for 1979 and just recently, last week, another report came out. What are they telling us? Our Economic Council is set up to give to politicians advice other than the one they get from the Department of Finance. It is warning Canadians that a peculiar phenomenon is taking place in Canada. This peculiar phenomenon is that instead of doing what you are supposed to do according to the text book in this inflationary period of going out and buying everything today because it will be worth twice as much tomorrow, Canadians do not do that. From 1975 to 1979 Canadians have doubled their rate of savings.
We were the leading saving nation in the world in 1975. We were saving at the rate of around 4.5 per cent and 5 per cent of our disposable income. Now we are saving at over 10 per cent. Canadians do not fit into the text book that the economists have down at the Department of Finance. Do you realize what 10 per cent of the disposable income of this nation is in a year? Our banks, our credit unions, our mortgage companies and our trust companies are bulging with money. They are in the tightest financial squeeze in our history. The more money you borrow at these high rates that they are offering, the greater the liabilities they have to make. If they cannot get this large amount out, the little guy goes down. Already the bank statements and the mortgage statements show the downward trend of earnings. They are in a squeeze just like the government is. I am simply saying that reality will force them to follow the practice, which I hope will be taken up by this government, instead of following these silly myths.
As I said, these ideas are not new, and I can give you other precedents back in 1965, and so on. But I am trying to make the point to the House that we have before us legislation which is good amending legislation. The principle is sound, it has worked, it does not cost the government very much, and it helps the bankers get along with their boards of directors, with a government guarantee. They lose no money. It has helped farmers, it has helped small businessmen, it has helped exporters, and it has helped the housing people in CMHC. But when the facts change, let us be willing to change here in the House. Let us put the ideas before our ministers so they will stand up to the brilliant advisers on the monetary and fiscal policy and say, "This is the quantitative evidence, let us get on with it." 1 would be very surprised if they did not agree. They must be shaking from top to bottom when they look at the evidence of what they are doing to us. These are not evil men, just men drilled to stay in a pyramid and never get away from the attitude of uniformity.
I have spoken like this around here for 25 years, and the battle goes on-the battle has to go on because, as the member for Burlington said, this country is in good shape and the United States is in good shape. But let us get the government and financial institutions off our backs. They cannot object, because if they go the way I am suggesting-and I know the government wants them to go that way-they are going to make more money. They cannot stay mad at you if they are making more money. Also the government will get more taxes, and I could go on on that subject.
Small Businesses Loans Act
I think, Mr. Speaker, that I have said enough to indicate that the House is tired of these band-aids in the last ten or 15 years. Raising the amount from $75,000 to $100,000 for the individual is a pretty small band-aid for the small businessmen today. The $500,000 on the development bond is a little better. But the basic weakness is not the amount that is available; the basic weakness is that if you lead people, who have to borrow for inventory purposes or operational purposes and all other purposes, into borrowing at these high rates of 12 per cent, 14 per cent or 16 per cent. You destroy them and you destroy the country at the same time. In all seriousness I would like the minister to accept these ideas, first, as being worth while, second, as being constructive, and third as having worked before for many centuries, which I am willing to demonstrate.
If I may throw a little bit of erudition into the debate, Mr. Speaker, let me point out that this is the same debate as was carried on between Plato and his student, Aristotle. The two fellows argued for a lifetime. Things have not changed much in this world.
I am simply pointing out to you that there is an opportunity here, with good will on both sides of the House. We are not trying to gun the minister or the government down. Let the idea be considered. You cannot lose by trying it, because there is no way of losing.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak today on the Small Businesses Loans Act. It is of great regret to me personally that this represents only a small step of no great significance in the history of this nation because the problems are so much more fundamental. While I have to agree with this bill, I should like to put before the minister, with all good will, some ideas for him to consider. It is amazing, given the underlying structural problems, that although this is the second bill with which we are in this Parliament, we should be giving much more time to the major aspects. It is interesting that we have just come through a $60 million election. The increase under this bill is $25,000 for small businesses. If we had not had the election, we could have given 2,400 businesses the full $25,000.
The underlying structural problem which the government must face, and which I hope this minister will face, is the reality on energy. The simple fact of the matter is that Canada is not an independent nation with respect to oil. We are a major importer of oil. Yet the federal government is carrying on as if we were independent. The structural problem is not one of price, on which the government has made its decision and which we are now spending time debating. We are into a conflict which may well tear this nation apart if the central government tries to move in on our Alberta oil at the price it has set. This could rip the nation apart; the issue is not price, it is supply. A government which is really trying to provide leadership should be more concerned that we have supply.
As one goes out and talks to any small businessman, he will say that all he wants is certainty. He is not so much concerned with what the price is, but he needs to know what it is so that he can plan and take those steps down the road. By this facade

April 25, 1980
Small Businesses Loans Act
of keeping the price in Canada allegedly below the world price, we are causing an effect which is very serious in terms of conservation.
We could be conserving. We know that a world price would result in more conservation. We know that 50 per cent of world price is blocking the production of goods. We know that 50 per cent of world price is blocking the signals which go back to the real producers in this nation, that is, our farmers and our small businessmen. Those signals are being blocked.
One might say that it is the big oil companies which control the price. That is simply incorrect. In the province of Alberta we have over 700 oil and gas companies. Other than the big five, they are small businesses which employ husbands, wives and children-60, 70, up to 100 people employed by them. They are the people who make this nation go.
The first structural problem is with respect to supply and price. The government could go a long way if it would just recognize that the people of Alberta have already forgone revenues of $17 billion. The people of Alberta have given up about $3 billion in the export tax. Never in the history of this nation has one province been called upon to make such a massive contribution to our nation. Yet I do not hear any real words of thanks, words of appreciation, or even an acknowledgement from the minister that the province which made that contribution would be appreciated. What we have is the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) going out and immediately attacking the oil industry in Alberta, attacking the 695 small businesses which really get out and do the skilled expertise of the seismic work, the geological work, the production of oil and gas, the refining of it, and then distributing it to the market. That is the key. The small businesses do that, not the big ones.
In spite of the major contribution of over $20 billion from the province of Alberta, it has managed to save $6 billion in its magical fund called the heritage trust fund. It is that fund which is so distorting the relationship in the country, because it is thought by the people in central Canada and the east that it is a massive money tree and that anyone can pluck it. We need to realize that $6 billion is nothing more than one year's budget for the entire province of Alberta. As a result of the gross mismanagement of the Canadian economy by the government of this federal nation, that $6 billion would be used up in six months. Six months of deficit financing would use the entire fund from Alberta.
Why would there be such a concern that one government in the country is building up this pool of money? What this country needs is this pool of money in order to make capital investments. That is what the province of Alberta does with its heritage trust fund. A percentage goes into Alberta industry and a percentage is allocated for Canadian industry. The types of investments required in this nation are what the Alberta heritage trust fund can undertake. Surely it is better to borrow the money from one of our own provinces which then keeps the interest circulating within our own country, rather than all of
us going off and borrowing in New York, Tokyo and Germany as we are right now.
I am moved to ask what price we as Canadians would be paying for our oil if that oil were located in the province of Quebec. I submit that the cabinet and the government would be much less aggressive in its attacking of the people of Quebec than it is the people of Alberta. I suppose the same applies to Ontario. I am moved to say that because I watched the members from Quebec make a major power move with respect to the F-18A at a time when our nation is at a critical stage vis-a-vis Quebec and the rest of the country. But there is also another dynamic, the dynamic between a central government and a provincial government like Alberta. I submit that the cabinet would have been much less aggressive in attacking Quebec members standing up and wanting that oil at 50 per cent than it has been with the people of Alberta.
The second major structural defect in our nation is simply the question of a balanced budget. I do not need to tell Mr. Speaker that the accumulated deficit is something in the order of $70 billion. The most recent budget of April 21 predicted a $14 billion deficit for one year. As well, Mr. Speaker knows that last year the United States had a deficit of $14 billion. That resulted in an immediate movement of citizens to convene a constitutional convention to block deficit financing at that level. But for the United States to be at a comparable debt level to us, it would have to have a yearly debt of $140 billion. They had a mere $14 billion and they are moving. We have $14 billion and our government seems to be proud of it.
The critical aspect of the budget deficits which affects small business is that we know as an actual fact that every nation only has a fixed amount of capital, and that different parts of that nation draw upon that capital in order to make the nation grow and prosper. Historically governments have always had a small part of that capital. That has left the rest of the capital for small business and creative people to use, to invest, to make more jobs, and to have more taxes flowing into the central government. What has happened, as a result of the Liberals taking power in 1968 and having no parliamentary responsibility for our budget, is that we have built up this massive deficit of $70 billion with a yearly deficit of $14 billion.
I wonder how many Canadian people genuinely realize that the amount of money we spend each year on interest to service the debt, without paying one cent of capital, is larger than the entire federal budget of 1968. I wonder if our friends in the NDP genuinely understand that their honest concern for the small man is frustrated by their collusion with the Liberal government in getting us into this deficit, because the people they purport to help, the small man or the person who is trying to keep the country together, is the person who is hurt the most by these massive deficits and high interest rates. As a result of the government making such a demand on our capital markets, it has had to compete. The government competes unfairly because it borrows money and it pays high interest rates with which small business cannot compete. That too is another major, underlying structural change.
April 25, 1980

We are talking about constitutional change. We hope we can keep this nation together. As members of Parliament, 1 would hope that each one of us would be pushing for a constitutional amendment which would force governments into balanced budgets, and that there would be no such thing as a deficit budget unless we were in times of a national economic crisis, war, depression or something really major, and not for the ongoing daily operations of governments.
I know the Liberal government has had quite a desire to spend but not to collect taxes. Not meaning to lecture, we all know the theory is that any group of social people have to create a government in order to make those decisions. The government, in its wisdom, comes up with programs, and it finances those programs by levying taxes on the citizens. In theory the government convinces people of the program need, and they are, therefore, willing to pay. If they are unhappy with either the programs or the amount of taxes, they vote people out.
We also know that in this nation over the last ten years the Liberal government has developed a system of being able to get money from the people, put programs in without having to tax people directly, and they do that by the mechanism of the Canada Savings Bond. They borrow money from their own citizens and pay them a return. They pay them not only the capital but they pay them interest, and the interest is borne by all of us.
I wonder how many people realize that in this last week $218 million in Canada Savings Bonds were redeemed, with $116 million redeemed the week before, as compared to a normal week when there is only $20 million being switched? The reason is simple. People are now realizing that the nation is in deep trouble and that they have to put their money in more secure sources, sources that will perhaps bring them a higher return.
Another way the government fools us is by going into the international market. When I told you a few minutes ago that we spend over $10 billion in interest alone, I neglected to say that the vast bulk of that money goes out of this country to service the debt in New York, Tokyo or Geneva.
The New Democratic Party actively colluded with the government to get us into that position, yet this is hurting the small man they purport to represent. They would have you believe, sir, that the amount of money that is leaving is really that of multinationals sending out interest and dividends to their head offices. This is sheer, unadulterated nonsense, because that is not correct. The bulk of the money leaving this country is interest the government itself is having to pay.
If instead of going into deficit financing, which is so hurting the small businessman today, the government had even increased taxes honestly, we would have been better off. If you take ten million taxpayers and they each pay $1,000, that is $10 billion of revenue per year.
In summary, while I have to say that I am fully in favour of this bill going through, I want the minister to consider honestly
Small Businesses Loans Act
the thought that it is a small stop-gap measure, that the real solution is not in amending the Small Businesses Loans Act, but instead it is in directing our efforts nationally to the question of supply of energy and directing our efforts to the size of government and the amount of money that government pulls out of our economy. If we had less government involvement in the money markets we would have more money available for small businesses which are really the backbone of this country, as the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) pointed out so well. They are the backbone, taking a little bit of money, hiring a dozen people who are all working hard toward a common objective, this resulting in taxes for us as members of Parliament to spend.
I wish the minister well in his efforts to convince the cabinet to solve the problems associated with energy supply and to direct its efforts to the size of government and the economic market, because if he is not successful the nation clearly is in deep trouble.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to comment on Bill C-17, the Small Businesses Loans Act amendment which we in the New Democratic Party will support with the clear understanding, however, that this is really not a full solution to the problems of small businesses.
When we speak of small business we are speaking of quite a range of economic activities, including manufacturing, the wholesale and retail trade, service businesses, construction, transportation and communications. In the case of this legislation, all of these businesses would have to be of less than $1.5 million in annual revenues.
The amendment proposes to raise the ceiling for loans under this act from $75,000 to $100,000. This is an increase of 25 per cent, yet inflation during the period from 1977 to 1980 went up by 30 per cent. Raising the ceiling under this legislation does no more than take care of the inflation rate since the ceiling was last established.
Loans are provided at the prime rate plus 1 per cent. This provision, however, is not used that widely. Many more loans are given at a higher rate because lending institutions can make a greater return outside the act. In 1979, small businesses borrowed something like $9 billion, whereas under this act the money that will be available is something like $425 million, so that we are talking about a small percentage of the loans to small business. Therefore we must do something to increase the use of this program.
I think there are a number of ways of coming to that, and one is to make small business more aware of the availability of these loans. Another way of coming to it is to encourage banks to use the act more aggressively. The Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe) could pressure the superintendent of banks to encourage greater use of this act and the program.
The amendment has limitations to the extent that the impact on interest rates will be minimal. It will be something in the order of .5 per cent to 1 per cent. That is not sufficient, given the very high interest rates we have today.

April 25, 1980
Small Businesses Loans Act
In addition, the loans under this act are available only for expansion of equipment, premises and land. There is no availability of loans under this legislation for operating capital. We should, therefore, be considering expanding the scope of this Small Businesses Loans Act to include operating capital.
As well, this amendment to this legislation is no substitute for sane interest rates. We need generally low interest rates in order to ensure access to capital for small business for all purposes.
The raising of the ceiling for loans under this legislation is also no substitute for sound economic policies, and it is no substitute for a growing economy, for one of the things that small business needs most is a demand for its services and a market for its goods. Because of the limited capital on which small businesses operate, they are very vulnerable to economic downturn and recession, and that certainly is the state of our economy at this point. Raising the ceiling under this legislation also does not in any way replace the need for a general and comprehensive business policy.
The New Democratic Party has many suggestions in this area which we would encourage the government to pick up on. For example, government procurement policy should favour small business. In the United States one-third of such procurement goes to small business, and we should do the same here.
The Economic Development Corporation should be helping small business find overseas markets. Research and development grants must be available, particularly in the area of high technology. Affordable capital must be made available for small businesses, whatever the purpose. A "buy-Canada" policy should be developed which will encourage large corporations in Canada to buy from small Canadian businesses. Also, when we come to the bill dealing with amending the Bank Act, which we will be dealing with next week, we must ensure that sufficient capital is allocated for small business. A great deal could also be done in the area of freeing up small business from the very heavy paper load under which they presently labour. NDP policy also deals with misleading advertising which would protect small business against unfair competition.
The need for a small business policy is very clearly evident from the present jump in the rate of bankruptcies in Canada. In the early part of this year, bankruptcies went up by 24.8 per cent over the same period last year. Clearly this demonstrates the need to help the small business community. This increase in the rate of bankruptcies brings the whole matter much closer to home for me because the economy of Manitoba, to a large extent, is made up of small businesses, particularly the economy of Winnipeg. For example, by way of statistical illustration, over 75 per cent of the 20,000 businesses in Manitoba are small businesses. Approximately 80 per cent of the 1,300 manufacturing companies in Manitoba are small businesses. A strong and sound small business policy is very crucial to the future of Manitoba.
Small business contributes a great deal to community life because those who run these small businesses live in the
community, are committed to it, and are not likely to pick up their business and go elsewhere. These people are residents and are an asset to the community. Small business is important, not only to Manitoba, but to Canada as a whole. Businesses with assets of less than $1 million constitute 90 per cent of the firms in Canada and over 50 per cent of the labour force. In this context it is necessary to take note of present economic conditions. The recession which Canada faces today creates very high unemployment, reduces the market for the services of small business, and points once again to the need for policies that will help small business, policies which will stimulate the economy and bring about sane interest rates.
Once again, I would indicate that my party will be supporting this legislation, but, while it is a good measure, it is by no means to be mistaken for a sufficient measure.
